strengths: Well-motivated and timely contribution: addresses the practical bottleneck of diffusion/flow-based RL policies (slow multi-step sampling) by adopting MeanFlow models, and carefully identifies and solves the two key technical obstacles (intractable likelihood, unavailable target samples) needed to integrate MeanFlow into soft policy iteration.

The proposed average divergence network (ADN) is a clever and efficient adaptation of the MeanFlow idea (average velocity -> average divergence) to make action likelihood tractable with only ~5% training overhead, and its accuracy is empirically validated against a 1000-step Euler reference (App. E.3) and on a 2D toy GMM task (App. E.1).

The adaptive instantaneous velocity estimation combining two SNIS proposals (Gaussian and current-policy) with ESS-based weighting is a principled and practically motivated solution to the exploration-vs-accuracy tradeoff across the ODE time horizon, supported by both an ESS/variance analysis (Fig. 1) and a bias/variance derivation (App. B.4).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning MuJoCo, DeepMind Control Suite, and HumanoidBench, with comparisons to 6 diffusion-based baselines and 2 classical baselines, plus supplementary comparisons to GMM and normalizing-flow policies (App. E.5) and a multi-modal AntMaze demonstration (App. E.6) that convincingly illustrates the benefit of combining expressive MeanFlow policies with MaxEnt exploration versus plain BPTT or unimodal SAC.

Thorough and honest ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component (MeanFlow vs standard flow, ADN vs no ADN, proposal sampling ratio, distributional critic, action selection, temperature target) and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (sampling steps, K1/K2, N), which substantially strengthens the credibility of the design choices.

Clear efficiency gains are demonstrated concretely (Table 1: 2 sampling steps vs 16-20+ for baselines, competitive inference latency) alongside performance parity or improvement, directly supporting the paper's central efficiency claim.
weaknesses: The convergence analysis (App. B.5) relies on strong idealized assumptions (exact likelihood recovery, K1,K2 -> infinity for unbiased velocity estimation, and that the true Boltzmann policy lies exactly within the MeanFlow policy class) that are unlikely to hold in practice; the practical algorithm explicitly acknowledges this gap ("we assume the solutions are close in practice"), so the theoretical guarantees provide limited assurance beyond motivating the design.

The overall algorithm is fairly complex, requiring an additional average divergence network, a mixture of two importance-sampling proposals with several extra hyperparameters (K1, K2, N, ADN training), and a two-timescale training procedure; this adds implementation burden that is not obviously less than the "specialized architectural choices" the paper criticizes in SAC-Flow.

Performance gains over strong baselines (e.g., SAC-Flow, DACER, MaxEntDP) are often described as merely "comparable or superior" rather than consistently dominant, and with only 5 random seeds it is difficult to assess the statistical significance of many head-to-head comparisons, especially on tasks where curves visually overlap.

The action-likelihood approximation error relative to the 1000-step Euler reference (Fig. 6c) shows noticeable spikes (up to ~0.4 relative error) during training, raising questions about how reliably the entropy term and importance weights behave in the more difficult phases of optimization, though this is not deeply analyzed.

The paper's efficiency claim of ~50% training-time reduction, while real, is more modest than the dramatic reduction in sampling steps (2 vs 16-114) might suggest, since the additional networks (ADN, distributional critic) and multi-proposal SNIS computation add back some overhead; a more detailed breakdown of where training time is spent would strengthen the efficiency narrative.

Reproducibility depends on the promised code release, which is not visible/verifiable in this manuscript version (URL redacted), and several practical design choices (e.g., choice of K1:K2=1:2, N=2, T=2) appear tuned specifically on Ant-v3/HalfCheetah-v3 without clear guidance on whether these transfer robustly to the DMC/HumanoidBench tasks.
